solution:
The odd one out is the **generator**.

Fuse wire, a bad conductor and rubber gloves are all connected with electrical safety. The chapter describes the fuse wire as a precautionary measure: "As soon as high current flows in a circuit, the fuse wire melts and breaks the circuit and any mishap is avoided." A bad conductor (an insulator) and rubber gloves protect a person from a shock because they do not let the current pass through them.

A generator does no protective job at all. It is a device that produces electricity, in which "mechanical energy is used to rotate the current carrying coil in a magnetic field, around an axle, thereby producing electricity." So it belongs to a different group from the other three.

[Note: rubber gloves and the term "bad conductor" are not discussed in this chapter's text; the safety role of the fuse wire is. The grouping above rests on that.]

The odd one out is the **thermometer**.

A voltmeter, an ammeter and a galvanometer are all electrical measuring instruments, and the chapter states that they share a single working principle: "Galvanometer is a sensitive device which works on the same principle as that of an electric motor that we have studied earlier... Voltmeter and Ammeter also work on the same principle." In each of them a coil placed between the poles of a magnet turns when a current passes through it, and the rotation is proportional to the current.

A thermometer measures temperature. It is not an electrical measuring instrument and it does not work on the motor principle, so it does not belong with the other three.

The odd one out is the **magnet**.

A loudspeaker, a microphone and an electric motor are all devices — each is a complete appliance built to do a job, and in each of them an electric current and a magnetic field act on one another. The chapter explains this for the motor: it is "A device changing electrical energy into mechanical energy", and it works because "whenever current flows through a conductor in the presence of magnetic field a force is exerted on the conductor."

A magnet is not a device. It is a component used inside such devices to supply the magnetic field, and it produces that field by itself without any electric current.

[Note: this chapter does not mention a loudspeaker or a microphone anywhere in its text — they appear only in this exercise. What the chapter does teach is the electric motor and the magnet used inside it, and the grouping above rests on that case.]

**Principle:** an electric motor is "A device changing electrical energy into mechanical energy." It works on the fact that a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force, whose direction is given by Fleming's left hand rule.

**Construction:** the motor consists of a rectangular loop (coil) of copper wire having a resistive coating. It is placed between the north pole and the south pole of a magnet (such as a horse-shoe magnet) in such a way that its branches AB and CD are perpendicular to the direction of the magnetic field. The two ends of the loop are connected to the two halves X and Y of a split ring. The two halves have a resistive coating on their inner surfaces and are tightly fitted on the axle. Their outer conducting surfaces are in contact with two stationary carbon brushes E and F, through which the loop is joined to a cell.

**Working:** when the circuit is completed, the current flows in branch AB from A to B through the carbon brushes E and F. Since the direction of the magnetic field is from the north pole to the south pole, by Fleming's left hand rule a force is exerted on branch AB which pushes it down. The current in branch CD is in the opposite direction, so the force on CD is directed upward. These two opposite forces turn the loop, and the loop and the axle start rotating in an anticlockwise direction.

After half a rotation, the two halves X and Y of the split ring come into contact with the carbon brushes F and E respectively, so the current in the loop now flows in the direction DCBA. A force is therefore exerted on branch DC in the downward direction and on branch BA in the upward direction, and the loop continues to rotate in the same anticlockwise direction. Thus the current in the loop is reversed after each half rotation and the rotation continues in one direction.

**Diagram (fig 4.13):** draw the rectangular coil ABCD between the N and S poles of the magnet, and label the coil, the north and south poles, the two split-ring halves X and Y, the two carbon brushes E and F, the axle and the cell.

**Principle:** an electric generator works on electromagnetic induction — "mechanical energy is used to rotate the current carrying coil in a magnetic field, around an axle, thereby producing electricity." The direction of the induced current is given by Fleming's right hand rule.

**Construction (fig 4.20):** a copper wire coil ABCD is kept between the two pole pieces of a magnet. The two ends of the coil are connected to the conducting rings R1 and R2 via carbon brushes. Both the rings are fixed to the axle, but there is a resistive coating in between the ring and the axle. The axle is rotated with the help of a machine from outside. The stationary carbon brushes B1 and B2 are connected to a galvanometer, which shows the direction of the current in the circuit.

**Working:** on rotating the axle, the branch AB goes up and the branch CD goes down, i.e. the coil ABCD rotates. By Fleming's right hand rule the induced current is produced in the branches in the directions A to B and C to D, so the current flows round the coil in the direction A to B to C to D, and in the external circuit it flows from B2 to B1 through the galvanometer.

After half a rotation the branch AB takes the place of branch CD and CD takes the place of AB, so the induced current now goes in the direction D to C to B to A. But the branch BA is always in contact with the brush B1 and the branch DC with B2, so in the external circuit the current now flows from B1 to B2, that is, opposite to the previous half rotation. "This repeats after every half rotation and alternating current is produced. This is what is called an AC generator."

If a coil of several turns is used instead of a single loop, a current several times larger is obtained.

**Diagram (fig 4.20):** draw the coil ABCD between the N and S poles, and label the coil, the magnetic field, the two conducting rings R1 and R2, the carbon brushes B1 and B2, the axle and the galvanometer.

Both machines convert mechanical energy into electrical energy by rotating a coil in a magnetic field, and both work on electromagnetic induction. They differ in the arrangement that joins the coil to the external circuit, and therefore in the kind of current they deliver.

| Point of difference | AC generator | DC generator |
|---|---|---|
| Connection of the coil to the brushes | The two ends of the coil are joined to two separate conducting rings R1 and R2, both fixed on the axle | A single ring cut into two halves — a split ring — is fixed on the axle, "like a split ring used in electric motor" |
| Contact with a given brush | Each branch of the coil stays joined to its own ring, so after every half rotation a given brush is fed by the branch that has moved to the other side | "the branch of the coil going upwards is always in contact with one brush and the branch going downwards is always in contact with the other brush" |
| Direction of current in the external circuit | Reverses after every half rotation — the current flows from B2 to B1, then from B1 to B2, and so on | Does not reverse: "the current flows in one direction in the external circuit" |
| Nature of the output current | Alternating current, which changes "in magnitude and direction after equal intervals of time" and is oscillatory | Direct current, which flows in one direction only; it "can increase, can be stable, or can reduce also, but it is not oscillatory" |

So the one real change in construction — two separate rings replaced by one split ring — is what decides whether the machine gives AC or DC.

**How a short circuit is formed:** the home electrical connection consists of 'live', 'neutral' and 'earth' wires. The 'live' and the 'neutral' wires have a potential difference of 220 V between them, and the 'earth' is connected to the ground. "Due to a fault in the equipment or if the plastic coating on the 'live' and the 'neutral' wires gives way, the two wires come in contact with each other." When the two wires touch directly, the current no longer has to pass through the resistance of an appliance; the resistance of the path becomes very small, and by Ohm's law \(I = V/R\) a very large current flows. This is a short circuit.

**Its effect:** "a large current flows through it producing heat", because by Joule's law of heating the heat produced is \(H = I^{2} R t\) and it grows as the square of the current. "If any inflammable material (such as wood, cloth, plastic etc.) exists around that place it can catch fire." This is why buildings sometimes catch fire due to a short circuit.

**The precaution:** a fuse wire is used in the circuit — "As soon as high current flows in a circuit, the fuse wire melts and breaks the circuit and any mishap is avoided." In homes a miniature circuit breaker (MCB) is also used: "When the current in the circuit suddenly increases this switch opens and current stops."

An electric bulb works on the heating effect of the electric current, and the filament has to become hot enough to glow. For such uses the chapter says that "Electrical conductors having higher resistivity are used here", and it names the metal: "a tungsten wire is used in an electric bulb. Because of the current, this wire gets heated (to nearly \(3400\ ^\circ\text{C}\)) and emits light. The hot wire also radiates heat to a certain extent."

So tungsten is chosen because it can be raised to that very high temperature and go on emitting light steadily without breaking, and because its resistivity is high enough for the current to heat it strongly.

The wire is wound into a solenoid-type coil (and that coil is wound again as a "coiled coil", fig 4.3) so that a long length of wire, and therefore a large resistance, is packed into the small space inside the glass bulb. By \(H = I^{2} R t\), the larger resistance gives more heat and hence more light.

[Note: the chapter gives the working temperature of about \(3400\ ^\circ\text{C}\) but does not state the melting point of tungsten.]

These appliances are made in order to produce heat. By Joule's law of heating the heat produced is \(H = I^{2} R t\), so for a given current the heating element must have a large resistance if a large amount of heat is to be obtained.

The chapter states exactly this and names the material: "Electrical conductors having higher resistivity are used here. For example, a coil made up of an alloy Nichrome is used in the electric heater-cooker as a resistor." A pure metal such as copper has a very low resistivity — it is used in this chapter for the connecting wires and the coils precisely because it carries a current with hardly any heating — so a pure metal would give very little heat and would be useless as a heating element.

[Note: the chapter states that a conductor of higher resistivity is needed for heating and that the element chosen is the alloy Nichrome, but it does not itself state the general rule that an alloy has a higher resistivity than the pure metals it is made from, nor does it discuss the melting point or the oxidation of the element. Those reasons are therefore not claimed here.]

A transmission wire has to carry current over long distances, and any resistance in the line turns some of the electrical energy into heat, which is wasted: by Joule's law of heating \(H = I^{2} R t\). To keep this loss small the transmission wire must have a very low resistance, and therefore be made of a material of very low resistivity.

This is exactly the opposite of what is wanted in a heating appliance, and the chapter states the contrast from that side: for the equipment that is meant to produce heat, "Electrical conductors having higher resistivity are used here." So for carrying current without producing heat, a conductor of low resistivity is required. Copper is such a conductor, and the chapter uses copper wire throughout its own experiments as the conducting wire — the "thick copper wire" passed through the cardboard, the "flexible copper wire" in the force experiment, and the copper coils of the motor and the generator.

[Note: the chapter never names aluminium at all, and it does not state the low-resistivity reason directly; the reason above is reached from its own statement that high-resistivity conductors are the ones chosen when heat is wanted. Separately, the chapter does say that "When the electric power is transmitted over a long distance, it is beneficial to have it in AC form as it results into minimum power loss during transmission" — but that is about the form of the current, not about the metal of the wire.]

The joule is far too small a unit for the quantities of electrical energy that are used in practice.

The chapter first makes this point about power: "The unit of electric power 1W is a very small unit, hence 1000 W or 1 kW is used as a unit to measure electric power, in practice." It then shows how large the practical unit of energy is:

\(1\ \text{kWh} = 1\ \text{kilowatt hour} = 1000\ \text{W} \times 3600\ \text{s} = 3.6 \times 10^{6}\ \text{Ws} = 3.6 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J}\)

So one kilowatt-hour is 3.6 million joules. Measuring a household's monthly consumption in joules would need enormously large and awkward numbers, whereas in kWh it is a small, convenient figure.

This is also why the electricity bill is made out in 'units': "When 1 kWh electrical energy is used, it is termed as 1 unit of energy."

**What a solenoid is:** "When a copper wire with a resistive coating is wound in a chain of loops (like a spring), it is called solenoid." When an electric current passes through it, magnetic lines of force are produced around it in a definite pattern (fig 4.9).

**Comparison with the field of a bar magnet.** The chapter states the resemblance directly: "The properties of the magnetic field of a solenoid are very similar to the magnetic field produced by a bar magnet."

- **Poles.** "One of the open ends of a solenoid acts as a magnetic north pole and the other as the magnetic south pole", just as a bar magnet has a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other.
- **Lines of force outside.** In both, the lines of force emerge from the north pole and return to the south pole, giving the same outward pattern.
- **Lines of force inside.** "The magnetic lines of force inside the solenoid are parallel to each other." This means "the intensity of the magnetic field within the solenoid is uniform everywhere, i.e. the magnetic field in a solenoid is uniform."
- **Strength.** The field of a solenoid depends on the current and on the number of turns — "if there are n turns in the loop, the magnetic field n times of that produced by a single loop will be created" — so it exists only while the current flows and can be made stronger or weaker at will. A bar magnet's field is always present and is not controlled in this way.

**Figures and components to name.** Draw the solenoid as a spring-shaped coil connected to a cell, with the magnetic lines of force drawn straight and parallel inside it and curving outside from one open end to the other; mark the open ends N and S. Beside it draw a bar magnet with its lines of force, and mark its N and S poles. Components to be named: the solenoid (coil of insulated copper wire), the cell, the magnetic lines of force, and the north and south poles in each figure.

[Note: the chapter stresses the similarity between the two fields and does not itself set out a list of differences; the last point above follows from its own statements about the field produced by a current.]

This diagram represents **Fleming's right hand rule**.

The hand drawn is the right hand. This can be checked against the chapter's own figures: fig 4.17, captioned "Fleming's right hand rule", draws the hand with the wrist at the right and the forefinger stretched out towards the left, exactly as here, while fig 4.11, captioned "Fleming's left hand rule", is its mirror image with the wrist at the left.

**The concept behind it.** The rule belongs to electromagnetic induction, and it is used to find the direction of the current induced in a conductor that is moved in a magnetic field — the principle of the electric generator. The chapter states it as follows: "Stretch the thumb, the index finger and the middle finger in such a way that they will be perpendicular to each other. In this position, the thumb indicates the direction of motion of the conductor, the index finger the direction of the magnetic field, and the middle finger shows the direction of the induced current."

The induced current is greatest when the motion is at right angles to the field: "It will be maximum when the direction of motion of the electric conductor is perpendicular to the magnetic field." The chapter uses this rule to work out the direction of the current in the generator coil ABCD.

This diagram represents **Fleming's left hand rule**.

The hand drawn is the left hand. This can be checked against the chapter's own figures: fig 4.11, captioned "Fleming's left hand rule", draws the hand with the wrist at the left and the forefinger stretched out towards the right, exactly as here, while fig 4.17, captioned "Fleming's right hand rule", is its mirror image with the wrist at the right.

**The concept behind it.** The rule belongs to the magnetic effect of an electric current. It is used to find the direction of the force that acts on a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field — the principle of the electric motor. The chapter states it as follows: "According to this rule, the left hand thumb, index finger, and the middle finger are stretched so as to be perpendicular to each other. If the index finger is in the direction of the magnetic field, and the middle finger points in the direction of the current, then the direction of the thumb is the direction of the force on the conductor."

The chapter then uses this rule to explain the working of the motor: the force on branch AB pushes it down, while the current in branch CD is in the opposite direction so the force on CD is upward, and the loop turns.

These are **electric fuses** — cartridge-type fuses, of the kind shown in fig 4.4 of this chapter, "Different types of fuses in use". The thin wire seen inside the glass body is the fuse wire, and the metal caps at the two ends are the contacts through which it is joined into the circuit.

**Use.** A fuse is put into a circuit as a safety device. If a fault such as a short circuit occurs, or the circuit is overloaded, a very large current flows; by Joule's law of heating \(H = I^{2} R t\) this current produces a great deal of heat, and "If any inflammable material (such as wood, cloth, plastic etc.) exists around that place it can catch fire."

The fuse wire is made so that it melts before that can happen: "Therefore, a fuse wire is used as a precautionary measure... As soon as high current flows in a circuit, the fuse wire melts and breaks the circuit and any mishap is avoided." Breaking the circuit stops the current at once and so protects both the wiring and the appliances. The chapter notes that for the whole house "the usual fuse wire is used", and that when too much current is drawn from the supply transformer "its fuse wire melts and the supply gets shut down. Such events occur due to overloading."

This is a **miniature circuit breaker (MCB)** — here a three-pole MCB of the kind mounted on a house distribution board, each of its three units carrying a switch marked OFF.

**Use.** It protects a circuit against an excessive current, as a fuse does, but it does so as a switch rather than as a wire that melts. The chapter says: "These days miniature circuit breakers (MCB) switches are used in homes. When the current in the circuit suddenly increases this switch opens and current stops."

So if a short circuit or an overload makes the current rise suddenly, the MCB opens by itself and disconnects that circuit, stopping the current before it can produce the heat that might otherwise set fire to anything nearby. The chapter adds that "Different types of MCBs are in use. For the entire house, however the usual fuse wire is used."

[Note: the chapter describes the MCB only as a switch that "opens" when the current increases. It does not say that the MCB can be switched on again after the fault is cleared, nor does it compare the MCB with the fuse on that point, so no such claim is made here. The word OFF is read from the printed photograph; the chapter's text does not contain it.]

This is an **electric generator of the DC type**.

The figure carries no labels, so it is identified from what is drawn: a rectangular coil turning between two magnet pole pieces; the two ends of the coil taken down to a ring fitted on the axle which is broken into two halves — a split ring; a stationary brush touching that ring on either side; and an external circuit containing an ammeter and no cell. A coil turning in a magnetic field with no source anywhere in the circuit means the current is being produced, not supplied, so the machine is a generator; and it is the split ring, rather than two separate rings, that makes the output a direct current.

**Use.** A generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy: "mechanical energy is used to rotate the current carrying coil in a magnetic field, around an axle, thereby producing electricity." It works on electromagnetic induction, the direction of the induced current being given by Fleming's right hand rule.

The split ring is what makes it a DC machine, and the chapter explains exactly how: "a split ring is fixed on the axle like a split ring used in electric motor. Because of this arrangement, the branch of the coil going upwards is always in contact with one brush and the branch going downwards is always in contact with the other brush. Hence, the current flows in one direction in the external circuit. This is why this generator is called as a DC generator." The ammeter in the external circuit shows the current so produced.

**Given:** rate of production of heat (that is, the power) \(P = 100\ \text{W}\); current \(I = 3\ \text{A}\). **To find:** the resistance \(R\).

The heat produced in a resistance per unit time is its power. By Joule's law of heating, \(H = I^{2} R t\), so

\(P = \dfrac{H}{t} = I^{2} R\)

\(R = \dfrac{P}{I^{2}} = \dfrac{100}{3^{2}} = \dfrac{100}{9} = 11.11\ \Omega\)

**The value of the resistance is about \(11\ \Omega\).**

This agrees with the value printed in the textbook, (Ans : \(11\ \Omega\)).

[Textbook note: the book prints (Ans : 0.72A). The exact value is \(160/220 = 8/11 = 0.7272\ldots\ \text{A}\), so the correctly rounded two-decimal figure is \(0.73\ \text{A}\); the printed \(0.72\ \text{A}\) is that same number truncated rather than rounded. The magnitude is not in dispute.]

**Given:** two bulbs of power \(P_{1} = 100\ \text{W}\) and \(P_{2} = 60\ \text{W}\), working at a potential difference \(V = 220\ \text{V}\), connected in parallel. **To find:** the current in the main conductor.

Because the two bulbs are connected in parallel, each of them gets the full potential difference of \(220\ \text{V}\), and the power drawn from the mains is the sum of the two powers:

\(P = P_{1} + P_{2} = 100 + 60 = 160\ \text{W}\)

The electrical power is \(P = V \times I\), so the current drawn in the main conductor is

\(I = \dfrac{P}{V} = \dfrac{160}{220} = 0.727\ \text{A}\)

**A current of about \(0.73\ \text{A}\) flows in the main conductor.**

**Given:** a TV set of \(500\ \text{W}\) used for 30 minutes, and a heater of \(600\ \text{W}\) used for 20 minutes. **To find:** which spends more electrical energy.

Electrical energy is the product of power and time, \(E = P \times t\), so the comparison cannot be made on the power alone — the times are different too.

For the TV set: \(t = 30\ \text{min} = 0.5\ \text{h}\)

\(E_{1} = 500 \times 0.5 = 250\ \text{Wh} = 0.25\ \text{kWh}\)

For the heater: \(t = 20\ \text{min} = \dfrac{1}{3}\ \text{h}\)

\(E_{2} = 600 \times \dfrac{1}{3} = 200\ \text{Wh} = 0.20\ \text{kWh}\)

Since \(250\ \text{Wh} > 200\ \text{Wh}\), **the TV set spends more electrical energy.**

Note that the heater has the greater power but is used for a shorter time, so the smaller power used for longer wins. This agrees with the answer printed in the textbook, (Ans : TV Set).

**Given:** an electric iron of power \(P = 1100\ \text{W} = 1.1\ \text{kW}\), used for \(t = 2\ \text{h}\) every day, for the month of April, at a rate of Rs 5 per unit. **To find:** the expenses for the month.

Energy used in one day:

\(E = P \times t = 1.1 \times 2 = 2.2\ \text{kWh}\)

Since "When 1 kWh electrical energy is used, it is termed as 1 unit of energy", this is 2.2 units per day.

April has 30 days, so the energy used in the month is

\(2.2 \times 30 = 66\ \text{units}\)

Expenses \(= 66 \times 5 = \text{Rs}\ 330\)

**The electrical consumption expenses for the month of April will be Rs 330.**

This agrees with the value printed in the textbook, (Ans : Rs 330).
